L2-01.why: its'/it's are never-correct spellings, so B and D are throwaways; the real contest is singular 'its' (presumably NO CHANGE) vs plural 'their'. Canonical its/it's item shape suggests the text already reads 'its'. Coin-flip between A and C; went with A.

L2-02.why: Pure transition item with no stem and no passage - nothing in the option set discriminates. Picked 'As a result' only because it is the most frequent key among ACT transition choices and 'Otherwise' is almost never keyed. This is a guess.

L2-03.why: Redundancy item: B ('spins around in circles') and D ('spins as it rotates') are overtly redundant; C is the only concise option. Conciseness rule with two self-refuting distractors.

L2-04.why: Clause-joining item: B is a fused sentence, C is a mangled comma pile, so D (semicolon between two independent clauses) is the only mechanically legal join. NO CHANGE is unseen but the alternates' shape says the error is a run-on.

L2-05.why: All three visible alternates carry a comma after 'hard' that splits the compound subject from its verb; since none of them may duplicate NO CHANGE, NO CHANGE is most likely the comma-free version, which is the correct one. Also A/C/D differ only in verb form, a classic 'all alternates share the same planted error' pattern.

L2-06.why: A ('and she offered') and C (semicolon) are both correct if the first part is an independent clause - two correct options is impossible, so the first part must be dependent (e.g. 'When she was sixteen'). That makes plain comma B uniquely legal. Solved by elimination-by-contradiction, not by reading.

L2-07.why: Vague-pronoun family: 'it', 'this' and (presumably) NO CHANGE all leave the referent unstated; C is the only option that names a noun. The key in this family is always the one that replaces the pronoun.

L2-08.why: '; and' (A) is illegal, which kills one. Between B (no comma) and C (paired commas around 'within a year') I cannot tell without the sentence; leaned to B on the ACT default that an unneeded comma is the planted error. Effectively a guess.

L2-09.why: Register/wordiness spread: B is slangy, D is pompous circumlocution, so the neutral plain-English option A is the key. NO CHANGE unseen but the two flanking extremes mark A as the intended middle.

L2-10.why: The phrase 'sometimes by several feet a year' is a parenthetical needing commas on both sides; A closes it wrong, C uses an illegal semicolon, D misplaces the first comma. None of the visible options is the correct both-commas version, so NO CHANGE must be it.

L2-11.why: Transition item, no stem, no passage - the option set carries no signal. 'In fact' chosen as a weak prior. Guess.

L2-12.why: Appositive-introduction family: 'being' (A) is the classic ACT wrong participle, the period (B) risks a fragment, so the colon (D) is the intended punctuation for introducing the named example.

L2-13.why: Subject-verb item: C inserts a comma between subject and verb, D a semicolon before a bare verb (both illegal); B is the clean 'cluster encodes'. Since B may not duplicate NO CHANGE, NO CHANGE must carry some other defect.

L2-14.why: Tense-only spread (have fallen / will have fallen / fall / NO CHANGE). Without the time markers in the sentence nothing decides it; present perfect is the most commonly keyed of these. Guess.

L2-15.why: Sentence-placement item: the options are bare 'Point A/B/C/D' labels with the referents scrambled across letters. There is literally zero information in the option set. Pure guess.
